## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Naṅgalīsajātaka* (Ja 123) is a Jātaka tale belonging to the late sutta section of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional framing narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha recounted the story while residing at Jetavana with reference to the elder Lāḷudāyi (Udāyi), who was notorious for habitually speaking inappropriately and uttering the wrong phrases at social gatherings [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1877].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta was an acclaimed world-renowned teacher (*disāpāmokkho ācariyo*) in Benares instructing young Brahmins [Law 1931; Fausböll 1877]. Among them was a dull-witted youth who, when prompted to report on what he observed in the forest, began comparing everything he encountered to a ploughshaft (*naṅgalīsa*)—initially describing a snake as resembling a ploughshaft, but subsequently applying the same simile indiscriminately to an elephant, as well as to curds and milk [Fausböll 1877]. Recognizing the youth's inability to comprehend that words and comparisons must not be used indiscriminately, the teacher spoke a verse on universal or inappropriate speech (*asabbatthagāmivācā*) and dismissed him [Fausböll 1877]. In the story's conclusion (*samodhāna*), the foolish student is identified as Lāḷudāyi and the teacher as the Buddha [Fausböll 1877].

Scholars have drawn on this Jātaka in different contexts: Naomi Appleton highlights it as a representative example of a common narrative template where a figure's foolish actions in the present mirror their folly in a previous existence, focusing on the shortcoming of a character other than the Bodhisatta [Appleton 2010]. Bimala Churn Law notes the tale's pedagogical context, wherein observation of nature was employed to cultivate curiosity and inquiry [Law 1931].

Regarding parallels and text reuse, SuttaCentral lists no parallels for this narrative [SuttaCentral], and DharmaNexus computed match data registers no Pali-internal reuse or cross-language parallels with a score of 10 or greater [DharmaNexus].
